qs.q: A patient with refractory hypertension is found to have an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma. Which downstream renal tubular biochemical effect accounts for the characteristic metabolic alkalosis observed in this disorder?
o: Increased apical hydrogen ion secretion with potassium wasting
Enhanced reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in tubules
Upregulated sodium-chloride symport activity in distal tubules
Stimulation of alpha-intercalated cell proton pumps
Inhibition of basolateral chloride-bicarbonate exchangers
qs.e: Aldosterone stimulates principal cells to reabsorb sodium and excrete potassium and hydrogen ions, promoting metabolic alkalosis.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Clinical Biochemistry Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient presents with chronic hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis due to surreptitious diuretic abuse. Which nephron site is the primary target?
o: Glomerular filtration barrier basement membrane
Early distal convoluted tubule Na-Cl cotransporter
Proximal tubule brush border Na-H exchanger
Descending limb aquaporin water channel
Medullary collecting duct urea transporter
qs.e: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the early distal tubule, increasing distal sodium delivery and potassium wasting.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Physiology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An infant with a 48-hour history of intussusception is found to have persistent shock, metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria, and hypokalaemia. Which clinical factor is most directly responsible for the metabolic alkalosis and paradoxical aciduria?
o: Diarrhoeal loss of bicarbonate ions from the inflamed colon
Extensive fluid sequestration within the compressed vessels
Prolonged bilious vomiting leading to loss of gastric acid
Renal conservation of hydrogen ions due to dehydration
qs.e: Prolonged vomiting in intestinal obstruction leads to a loss of gastric hydrogen and chloride ions, resulting in hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria as the kidneys retain acid to excrete sodium. This is a classic electrolyte disturbance in prolonged cases.
qs.s: Intussusception in Children: Diagnosis, Air Enema and Surgery: MCQs

qs.q: A 3-week-old boy is evaluated for projectile vomiting. Laboratory results show hypochloraemia, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. What is the primary renal mechanism driving paradoxical aciduria in this condition?
o: Aldosterone blockade secondary to volume depletion
The kidney excretes hydrogen ions to conserve sodium
Primary renal tubular acidosis induced by dehydration
The kidney conserves hydrogen ions over potassium
qs.e: In hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, the kidney conserves hydrogen ions at the expense of potassium, resulting in acid urine despite a systemic alkalosis. This is known as paradoxical aciduria.

qs.q: A 6-week-old infant with confirmed hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is being prepared for surgery. The patient has significant hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. What is the mandatory sequence of management before the Ramstedt pyloromyotomy can be performed?
o: Insertion of a nasogastric tube, then immediate Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
Correction of fluids and electrolytes, then Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
Administration of proton pump inhibitors, then Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
Immediate pyloromyotomy followed by post-operative fluid correction
qs.e: The note explicitly states that fluids and electrolytes must be corrected first, followed by the Ramstedt pyloromyotomy. Operating before correcting the metabolic derangement is contraindicated.

qs.q: A 4-week-old boy presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and a palpable epigastric mass. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
o: Correct fluid and electrolyte deficits before pyloromyotomy
Initiate aggressive oral rehydration therapy and feeds
Administer intravenous potassium and perform pyloroplasty
Perform immediate diagnostic laparoscopy and division
qs.e: Electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities must be fully corrected prior to surgery to minimize anesthetic risk. Pyloromyotomy is the surgical treatment, whereas pyloroplasty is used for peptic ulcer disease.

qs.q: A 5-week-old infant with confirmed infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis has persistent vomiting and visible gastric peristalsis. Initial blood gas analysis shows severe metabolic alkalosis with hypochloremia. What is the surgical readiness status of this patient?
o: Ready for immediate Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
Not ready until diagnostic laparoscopy is performed
Ready for surgery because vomiting is non-bilious
Not ready until fluids and electrolytes are corrected
qs.e: Electrolyte and fluid deficits must be completely restored before any surgical intervention is undertaken. Proceeding immediately without correction carries a high risk of postoperative apnea and arrest.

qs.q: An infant develops severe watery diarrhea starting on the first day of life. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, and a fecal chloride concentration that exceeds the sum of fecal sodium and potassium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Microvillous Atrophy
Congenital Sodium Diarrhea
Congenital Chloride Diarrhea
Autoimmune Enteropathy
qs.e: Congenital chloride diarrhea is characterized by hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis and high fecal chloride levels. Congenital sodium diarrhea presents instead with hyponatremia and metabolic acidosis.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Metabolic alkalosis is a primary increase in plasma bicarbonate that raises pH, usually from loss of gastric acid or excess alkali. The body compensates by hypoventilation, raising CO₂.

sections.p: A primary metabolic alkalosis is defined by pH > 7.45, HCO₃⁻ > 28 mmol/L and an elevated PCO₂ that matches the expected respiratory compensation (PCO₂ ≈ 0.7 × HCO₃⁻ + 20).
b: Diagnostic criteria: pH > 7.45, HCO₃⁻ > 28 mmol/L, PCO₂ appropriate to HCO₃⁻.

t.b: Is the alkalosis metabolic or respiratory? Shows pH, HCO₃⁻, PCO₂; appropriate compensation confirms primary metabolic alkalosis.
Are chloride and potassium low? Low Cl⁻ and K⁺ suggest chloride‑responsive (vomiting, diuretics) versus chloride‑resistant causes.
Is the alkalosis chloride‑responsive? Urine Cl⁻ < 20 mmol/L indicates volume depletion; ≥20 mmol/L suggests renal loss or alkali ingestion. If unavailable, infer from clinical volume status.

sections.p: Severity is graded by bicarbonate level and symptom burden: mild (28‑34 mmol/L, asymptomatic), moderate (35‑44 mmol/L, mild neuromuscular signs), severe (≥45 mmol/L, marked weakness, arrhythmia).
b: Mild: HCO₃⁻ 28‑34 mmol/L; moderate: 35‑44 mmol/L; severe: ≥45 mmol/L.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by loss of acid, gain of alkali, or renal retention. In most settings, vomiting and diuretic use are top, but tropical infections and herbal remedies also matter.
b: Vomiting or nasogastric suction – loss of HCl (most common).
Loop or thiazide diuretics – chloride‑responsive renal loss.
Excess alkali ingestion (antacids, milk‑alkali).
Hyperaldosteronism, Cushing’s, licorice – renal H⁺ retention.
Tubulopathies (Bartter, Gitelman) – especially in low‑resource areas.
Severe volume depletion from diarrhoea with concurrent alkali therapy.

sections.p: Patients often have nausea, vomiting, or a history of diuretic use, plus neuromuscular irritability (tetany, cramps) and cardiac arrhythmias from hypokalaemia.
b: Dry mucous membranes, orthostatic hypotension (volume depletion).
Muscle weakness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm (hypokalaemia).
Palpitations, prolonged QT or arrhythmias.

sections.p: Focused labs and bedside tests clarify the aetiology and severity, guiding therapy.

t.b: Is hypokalaemia present? Low K⁺ worsens alkalosis and predisposes to arrhythmia; replacement is essential.
Is renal K⁺ loss ongoing? High urine K⁺ (>20 mmol/L) indicates renal wasting (diuretics, hyperaldosteronism).
Is there pulmonary disease limiting hypoventilation? Absence of lung pathology supports primary metabolic alkalosis.

sections.p: Severe alkalosis can precipitate life‑threatening cardiac events and central nervous system depression.
b: Severe hypokalaemia (<2.5 mmol/L) → ventricular arrhythmias.
Very high bicarbonate (>45 mmol/L) → decreased cerebral blood flow, seizures.
Concurrent metabolic acidosis (mixed disorder) → masked pH changes.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct volume, chloride, and potassium deficits while monitoring electrolytes and pH.
b: Stop vomiting source; treat obstruction or give anti‑emetics.
Discontinue offending diuretics; switch to potassium‑sparing agents if needed.
IV isotonic saline restores volume and chloride, promoting renal bicarbonate excretion.
IV potassium chloride (or oral KCl) replaces K⁺; avoid rapid IV K⁺ without ECG monitoring.
If chloride‑resistant (e.g., hyperaldosteronism), give amiloride or spironolactone to block distal H⁺/K⁺ exchange.

sections.p: Re‑check electrolytes after each intervention, educate on medication use, and address chronic causes.
b: Daily serum electrolytes until stable.
Educate patients on proper diuretic dosing and need for potassium‑rich diet.
Screen for endocrine causes if alkalosis recurs.

sections.p: Conditions that also raise pH but have different mechanisms.
b: Respiratory alkalosis – primary low PCO₂, not high HCO₃⁻.
Mixed metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis – may show normal pH despite severe disorders.

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite serious disturbance.
b: Urine chloride can be low in early volume depletion, falsely suggesting renal cause.
Serum bicarbonate may be normal if a mixed disorder masks the alkalosis; always interpret with pH and PCO₂.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe weakness with arrhythmia or syncope
Persistent vomiting with inability to retain fluids
Sudden onset of seizures or altered mental status

faq.q: Why does vomiting cause metabolic alkalosis?
faq.a: Stomach acid (HCl) is lost, removing H⁺ and Cl⁻, leaving a relative excess of bicarbonate.
Low K⁺ drives H⁺ into cells, raising extracellular pH; kidneys also retain bicarbonate to conserve K⁺.

faq.q: When is saline preferred over bicarbonate therapy?
faq.a: In chloride‑responsive alkalosis, saline restores volume and chloride, allowing kidneys to excrete excess bicarbonate.

exam: Explain the physiological basis of respiratory compensation in metabolic alkalosis and calculate expected PCO₂ for a given HCO₃⁻.
List the three most common causes of metabolic alkalosis in a low‑resource setting and describe how you would differentiate them.
Describe the step‑wise management of a patient with hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis due to loop diuretics.
